svg.title: Arrays, the screen and strings
svg.desc: Five panels for the Lab 05 theory. 1: Byte buf[8] = {1, 2, 3}, eight cells with the rest zero; buf[i] is *(buf + i); buf[8] is past the end. 2: int m[3][4] as a table and as memory, k = r * 4 + c, m[1][2] is k = 6. 3: a 64 × 32 screen in 256 bytes from 0xA00: pixel (13, 2) is byte 0xA11, bit 2, mask 0x04; without “7 −” x = 10 lights up instead. 4: char s[4] = "HI" and strlen up to the first zero; "ABCD" with no room for the zero. 5: bubble sort on 4 1 3 2: six comparisons, four swaps.
svg.text: An array is memory in a row plus a rule for where element i lives. The rest follows from that rule.
1. An array is memory plus a rule
Byte buf[8] = {1, 2, 3}; // the rest are zeros
buf[i] is *(buf + i): the address of the first element plus i steps (Lab 3).
buf[8] is no longer the array: ASan stops the program.
Passed to a function, buf arrives as a pointer, so the size is passed separately:
2. Two dimensions are one dimension and a stride
a row sits together in memory
Walking by rows goes in order; by columns it jumps 4 elements
(16 bytes for int). The swapped formula c * 3 + r gives a different element.
3. A pixel is a bit: a 64 × 32 screen in 256 bytes
Pixel (13, 2). Formulas from ISA §7; the same numbers come from ./run.sh 03 13 2 in the Lab 05 practice.
pixel (13, 2): row 2, byte 1 of that row
without: x = 10, mirrored in its byte
strlen walks off the end: ASan
6 comparisons, 4 swaps. After each pass the largest of the rest is in place.
